    Summary and Setup

    This lesson is about Interoperability in Climate and Atmospheric Sciences. The value of scientific data depends not only on its scientific content but on how easily it can be found, accessed, integrated, and reused by others, whether they are human researchers or automated computational workflows.

    This course focuses on how to create first-class research outputs using the NetCDF format and publishing them through the 4TU.ResearchData repository. By following community best practices, these datasets can:

    • be easily found through rich, machine-actionable metadata,

    • be reliably accessed using open standards and stable identifiers,

    • be seamlessly integrated with other datasets and

    • be confidently reused .

    Throughout this course, you will learn how to produce NetCDF datasets that meet these standards, datasets that are not only scientifically valuable today, but that remain accessible, interoperable, and reusable for years to come.

    Target audience

    This lesson is intended for researchers in the climate and atmospheric sciences who handle multidimensional NetCDF datasets and intend to make their data and software more reusable by others.

    Use case

    In climate and atmospheric sciences, several well-curated, domain-specific data infrastructures play a foundational role. These include, for example, the Copernicus Climate Data Store, the National Centers for Environmental Information, the NASA EarthData, and the NCAR/UCAR Research Data Archive. These critical repositories continuously curate high-value reference datasets, from satellite retrievals and reanalyses to in-situ observations, and provide rich tooling for both humans and machines to access, filter, and process data at scale.

    Such specialized services are indispensable for Earth system research: they maintain consistent data models, harmonize metadata, ensure traceability of processing steps, and provide APIs that make it possible to programmatically retrieve and intercompare datasets. They also serve as long-term archives of essential climate variables used for monitoring, policy evaluation, and climate modeling.

    However, not all datasets in the climate and atmospheric science ecosystem can be deposited into such well-structured domain repositories. Many important datasets, especially those generated by individual research groups, short-term field campaigns, laboratory atmospheric experiments, model development teams, or niche sensor deployments, do not fit cleanly into the data models of these special-purpose repositories. Yet these datasets are no less important for integrative research, reproducibility, or long-term scientific value.

    As a result, researchers increasingly deposit their data into general-purpose data repositories, at scales ranging from institutional (e.g., university data hubs) to global platforms such as Zenodo, Figshare, Dryad, Dataverse, Mendeley Data, 4TU.ResearchData and EUDAT. These platforms accept almost any data format, generally do not enforce structural or semantic standards, and rarely validate whether the data is interoperable with existing community conventions. While this flexibility is important, it also means that the broader data ecosystem is becoming more heterogeneous and therefore less integrated, making discovery and reuse more difficult for both humans and computational workflows.

    Now, imagine Leo a researcher studying extreme heatwave events over Europe. Leo has produced a high-resolution convection-permitting regional climate model (RCM) simulation for two recent heatwave summers, and now wish to compare their model outputs with:

    • satellite-derived land surface temperature and soil moisture,
    • urban heat island observations from local sensor networks,
    • aircraft-based atmospheric profiles collected during a heatwave monitoring campaign.

    Where does Leo begin?

    The challenge quickly becomes apparent, the relevant datasets may be scattered across many platforms:

    • Satellite and reanalyses in special-purpose repositories (CDS, NASA EarthData, RDA)
    • Airborne campaign measurements in discipline-specific archives, if they exist at all
    • Local sensor network data in university repositories or GitHub pages
    • Urban meteorology datasets published in institutional or general-purpose repositories

    Searching for datasets requires filtering by spatial region (Europe), temporal range (heatwave periods), variables (temperature, soil moisture, humidity profiles), instrument types, model version, and metadata quality.

    But are these descriptors consistently captured? Are they machine-readable? Do repositories expose them through Application Programming Interfaces (APIs)? Sometimes yes, often no.

    Once datasets are found, they may appear in multiple formats:

    • NetCDF following CF conventions (easy to integrate)
    • CSV files with ambiguous column headers (hard for machines)
    • GeoTIFFs with incomplete coordinate metadata
    • Custom binary formats from aircraft instruments
    • Zipped folders containing Excel spreadsheets and undocumented metadata sheets

    Each format requires a different workflow, different tools, and often manual interpretation of metadata.

    Even when datasets use the same formats, semantics may differ:

    • One dataset reports temperature as T2M (Kelvin), another as temp_2m (Celsius).
    • Soil moisture might be expressed as volumetric, percent, or relative saturation, without clear units.
    • Spatial referencing may be explicit (CF-compliant) or vaguely described (“local grid”).

    Machine-actionable metadata is the exception, not the rule. What should take hours often takes weeks or months, not because the science is complex, but because the digital objects were not made FAIR, particularly not Interoperable, at the time of publication. These challenges highlight that interoperability is a prerequisite for modern climate and atmospheric science, where answering any meaningful research question often requires combining:

    • satellite + ground observations,
    • models + reanalyses,
    • global-scale + local-scale datasets,
    • products from multiple institutions, nations, and infrastructures.

    The obstacle is not a lack of technology: we have NetCDF-CF, ACDD metadata conventions, OPeNDAP, ERDDAP, THREDDS, ISO schemas, controlled vocabularies, and robust APIs. The real problem is that digital objects are not routinely created, curated, or archived following community interoperability standardss.

    The value of scientific data depends not only on its scientific content but on how easily it can be found, accessed, integrated, and reused by others, whether they are human researchers or automated computational workflows.

    To support future Leo, and every researcher who will build on today’s work, this course focuses on how to create first-class research outputs using the NetCDF format and publishing them through the 4TU.ResearchData repository. By following community best practices, these datasets can:

    • be easily found through rich, machine-actionable metadata,

    • be reliably accessed using open standards and stable identifiers,

    • be seamlessly integrated with other datasets and

    • be confidently reused .

    Throughout this course, you will learn how to produce NetCDF datasets that meet these standards—datasets that are not only scientifically valuable today, but that remain accessible, interoperable, and reusable for years to come.

    Learning objectives

    By the end of this lesson, learners will be able to:

    • Analyze climate and atmospheric datasets to distinguish interoperable from non-interoperable systems across structural, semantic, and technical layers.

    • Analyze a NetCDF dataset to evaluate how its data model, dimensions, variables, and metadata organization enable structural interoperability.

    • Evaluate the semantic interoperability of a NetCDF dataset using CF Conventions and explain how shared vocabularies enable machine-actionable meaning.

    • Apply OPeNDAP to access and subset remote NetCDF datasets, distinguishing between metadata retrieval and data transfer in distributed infrastructures.

    • Apply and analyze REST API principles to programmatically create and manage repository metadata, explaining how APIs operationalize technical interoperability.

    • Analyze how cloud-native data layouts (NetCDF vs Zarr) affect performance, scalability, and structural interoperability in distributed environments.

    • Evaluate a research data infrastructure against AI-readiness requirements by linking structural, semantic, and technical interoperability components to scalable machine learning workflows.

    Prerequisite

    To follow this lesson, learners should already be able to have :

    • Working knowledge in Python (write and execute short scripts in Python)
    • Awareness of NetCDF format

    Software Setup

    This course requires a working Python 3 environment, a Unix-like terminal, and several Python libraries used throughout the episodes.

    We strongly recommend setting up a dedicated virtual environment for this course.

    1. Python 3 Installation (required)

    Download the latest Python 3 version from:

    👉 https://www.python.org/downloads/

    The course has been tested with Python 3.11, but any currently supported version should work: https://devguide.python.org/versions/#versions

    ⚠️ Python 2.7 is not supported.

    Verify Your Installation

    Open a terminal and run:

    BASH 

    python3 --version   # macOS / Linux
python --version    # Windows

    Expected output (example):

    BASH 

    Python 3.11.4

    To confirm you are using the standard Python distribution:

    BASH 

    python3   # or python on Windows

    You should see something like:

    BASH 

    Python 3.11.4 (main, Jun 20 2023, ...)
>>>

    Exit with:

    BASH 

    exit()

    or CTRL+D.

    2. Create a Virtual Environment (Recommended)

    We use venv for environment isolation and pip for package management.

    Create a virtual environment:

    BASH 

    python3 -m venv nes-course-env

    Activate it:

    • macOS / Linux:

      BASH 

      source nes-course-env/bin/activate

    • Windows (PowerShell):

      BASH 

      nes-course-env\Scripts\Activate.ps1

    You should now see the environment name in your prompt.

    Upgrade pip:

    BASH 

    pip install --upgrade pip

    3. Core Python libraries (Required for most episodes)

    Install the core scientific stack:

    BASH 

    pip install xarray netCDF4

    These are used for:

    • Reading NetCDF datasets
    • Data analysis
    • Structural interoperability exercises

    4. Additional libraries for Cloud-Native layouts (Episode on Zarr & Kerchunk)

    For the cloud-native layouts episode, you will also need:

    • zarr
    • kerchunk
    • fsspec
    • netCDF4 (or h5netcdf)

    Install all required libraries with:

    BASH 

    pip install xarray zarr kerchunk fsspec netCDF4

    What is fsspec?

    fsspec (Filesystem Spec) is a Python library that provides a unified interface to multiple storage backends:

    • Local filesystem
    • HTTP / HTTPS
    • S3
    • Google Cloud Storage
    • Azure Blob
    • SSH
    • In-memory storage

    It enables libraries such as:

    • xarray
    • zarr
    • kerchunk
    • dask

    to access remote data as if it were a local filesystem.

    fsspec is often installed automatically as a dependency of kerchunk.

    What is kerchunk?

    kerchunk enables cloud-native access to NetCDF and HDF5 files without rewriting them to Zarr.

    It works by:

    1. Scanning a NetCDF/HDF5 file
    2. Extracting internal chunk metadata
    3. Creating a JSON reference description
    4. Allowing access via fsspec + xarray as if it were a Zarr dataset

    This allows:

    • Lazy loading
    • Parallel access
    • Cloud-optimized workflows
    • Avoiding expensive data conversion

    Kerchunk is especially relevant when:

    • You cannot rewrite original NetCDF files
    • Data is stored in object storage
    • You want to improve interoperability in cloud workflows

    5. Unix Terminal (Required for API Episodes)

    You will need a Unix-like terminal.

    Linux

    Native terminal is sufficient.

    macOS

    Use the default Terminal app.

    Windows

    Install one of:

    • Git Bash: https://git-scm.com/downloads
    • Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL): https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install

    6. API Command-Line tools (Required for REST API episodes)

    yq (Required)

    YAML processor used to manipulate metadata files.

    Linux

    BASH 

    sudo apt-get update
sudo apt install yq

    macOS

    BASH 

    brew install yq

    Windows (PowerShell)

    Install Scoop:

    BASH 

    Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri https://get.scoop.sh | Invoke-Expression

    Then:

    BASH 

    scoop install yq

    jq (Optional but recommended)

    JSON processor for nicely formatted API outputs.

    Linux

    BASH 

    sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y jq

    macOS

    BASH 

    brew install jq

    Windows

    BASH 

    scoop install main/jq

    Verify installation:

    BASH 

    yq --version
jq --version

    7. Recommended IDE

    You may use any editor, but we recommend:

    • Visual Studio Code (VS Code) https://code.visualstudio.com/

    Install the Python extension for best experience.
